summary:
Arequipa department has no region-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding on record. All three attached sources are national in scope, and as national measures they bind the department. The operative legal frame for a visitor to Arequipa is the national one.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The facility restriction is in force. The Commission on Women and Family approved a dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457 on 20 February 2025, barring entry to public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to one's birth sex, with exceptions only for custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and requiring unambiguous signage. The Congress plenary approved the package on 2 April 2025, exempt from a second vote, as article 5 of the law strengthening the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents; the wider package was enacted as Law 32331 on 13 May 2025. A trans traveller using a public restroom in Arequipa therefore faces a live national legal exposure.

Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho warned that the measure would leave security staff to judge people by personal criteria, such as requesting their national identity document. Enforcement of the restriction reaches private as well as public life: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told congresswoman Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report counted 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women most affected and hate crimes rising; its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The report recounts the February 2023 kidnapping of trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her murder in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang, the bodies showing gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting that indicate extreme hate.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard the facility restriction does not meet.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, finds that article 5 implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination. The same analysis notes that Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage, and records dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Vague child-protection articles, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
localsOnly:
Residents of Arequipa live under the same national facility rule as visitors, but the practical burden falls hardest on those who must present documents or justify their presence daily: the DNI check described by Gianna Camacho is a routine gatekeeping mechanism in workplaces, gyms and public buildings.

Two protective developments are on record nationally. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Arequipa-specific source was located. Whether the facility restriction has been enforced in the department, by which authority, and with what frequency is unresolved and not sourced here.

The 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases are national totals for 2020 to 2023; no breakdown by department exists in the inventory, so the share of that violence occurring in Arequipa is unresolved. The cited co-author states the recorded figures are a sub-registry, so the true count is higher than the record shows.

Entry, visa and document-marker rules for trans travellers arriving in Peru are not covered by any source in this inventory and remain not sourced. Whether the dismissed gym complaint was appealed, and the current status of the anti-equality decree litigation beyond the July 2025 ruling, are likewise unresolved.
